newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha dismisses absent Bank of Albania governor.
newsitem.headline: Berisha dismisses absent Bank of Albania governor.

text.p: President Sali Berisha has dismissed the governor of the Bank of Albania who left the country during an armed insurrection and replaced him with another senior banker, a central bank official said on Friday.
Berisha had appointed Qamil Tusha, previously number two at a state-run commercial bank, to replace Kristaq Luniku, who left Albania two months ago, the official said.

"The supervising board of the Bank of Albania...thought it was necessary to overcome this extraordinary situation by finding a replacement," the official, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.

In February this year an armed insurrection erupted across Albania, triggered by the collapse of "pyramid" investment schemes in which many people had invested their life savings. More than 300 people have been killed in the violence.

Central bank and presidency officials said that the supervising board of the Bank of Albania had chosen Tusha to replace Luniku and that Berisha had signed a decree this week confirming the appointment.
"Qamil Tusha has already taken up his duties as the new central bank governor with a seven-year appointment," presidency spokeswoman Linda Ihsani told Reuters.
Tusha was attending meetings at the central bank and was not immediately available.

Central bank sources said Tusha, who was previously deputy director of the National Commercial Bank, was a 39-year-old economics graduate of Tirana University, who had worked as a banker for more than a decade.

Carlos Elbirt, chief resident representative of the World Bank, told Reuters: "We hope that monetary policy will be conservative and appropriate in these difficult times. Stringency will be very important."
Press reports said that Luniku, a 34-year-old economist, was now working with the International Monetary Fund in Washington advising on the Albanian economy.
They said that Luniku had warned Berisha last year that legislation was urgently needed to ban the dubious "pyramid" schemes. Parliament banned the schemes in January.
Last December Luniku said in a press interview that sky-high interest rates offered by the pyramid schemes endangered the development of Albania's fledgling commercial banking system.
Albanian authorities are struggling to rebuild the economy since the rebellion as prices have soared and the lek currency has plunged.
Year-on-year inflation stood at 35.9 percent in March, after the uprising broke out, compared with a year-on-year rate of 16.9 percent in January.
Albania has approved no state budget for 1997.

Albania's economy will contract by between three and seven percent this year as a result of the violence, Edmond Leka, head of economic aid and development for Albania's council of ministers, said earlier this month.
